summary: Defines a YANG data model for Access Control Lists, ordered sets of rules that match packets and define actions on them, to configure forwarding behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: A guest list with rules: if the packet looks like this, let it in; if like that, block it. This is a standard form for the list.

questions: what is an access control list
what is the yang acl model
how does an ace match packets
what does the reject action do in an acl
subtitle: A standard YANG schema for writing access control lists: ordered rules that match packets and say what to do with them.

tldr.problem: Every vendor models access control lists differently, so configuring packet filters across devices means learning each vendor's own data model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8519 defines two YANG 1.1 modules: a generic ACL module and a packet-fields module. An ACL is an ordered list of entries, each pairing match criteria with actions, and the base model can be augmented for extra protocols or vendor features.
tldr.outcome: Vendors get a common base model for ACL configuration that they can extend, and they advertise what they support through feature statements.

today: RFC 8519 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What an Access Control List Is
sections.content:
An Access Control List (ACL) is one of the basic elements used to configure device-forwarding behavior. It is used in networking technologies such as Policy-Based Routing (PBR) and firewalls. An ACL is a user-ordered set of rules that filters traffic on a networking device, and each rule is an Access Control Entry (ACE).

Each ACE has a group of match criteria and a group of actions. Packet header matches apply to fields visible in the packet, such as an address, Class of Service (CoS) or a port number. Metadata matches, where a vendor supports them, apply to things not in the header, such as the input interface or the length of the packet as received.

An ACL does nothing until it is attached to something, such as an interface, a Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) interface, a vty/tty session, a QoS policy or a routing protocol. To attach an ACL to anything other than an interface, vendors would have to augment the model.
sections.plainLanguage: An ACL is a checklist a doorman follows. Each line on the list says what a visitor must look like and what to do about it.

sections.title: Common Ground and the Problem to Solve
sections.content:
The RFC defines a YANG 1.1 data model (RFC 7950) for configuring ACLs. It has matching rules for commonly used protocols: Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP. If more protocols are needed later, the base model can be augmented.

ACL implementations vary greatly between devices in the filters and actions they support. Vendors also have different ACL data models, but there is a common understanding: a system has a list of ACLs, and each ACL holds an ordered list of ACEs. The RFC therefore proposes a base model that standard extensions and vendor proprietary models can build on.

Actions can be any operation, from logging to rate-limiting, dropping or simply forwarding. Actions on the first matching ACE are applied, and later ACEs are not processed.
sections.plainLanguage: Different shops write their guest lists in different ways. This RFC picks one simple way that everyone can start from and then add their own special notes.

sections.title: Two Modules and Feature Statements
sections.content:
The model has two YANG modules. ietf-access-control-list defines the generic ACL aspects that are common to all ACLs whatever their type or vendor. The RFC describes it as a generic ACL "superclass". It imports ietf-packet-fields, whose groupings supply the match fields, such as port numbers or protocols.

Devices differ, so the model uses feature statements. One set says what the device can match on, for example Ethernet headers or IPv4 headers. A second set says which combinations of headers the device is willing to support, for example "Plain IPv6 ACL supported" or "Ethernet, IPv4 and IPv6 ACL combinations supported". Together with if-feature checks and must statements, they decide which match fields a user can define rules for.

The matches container can be augmented when something new is needed, and the RFC gives IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: A device tells the list-maker which kinds of checks it knows how to do, like a doorman saying he can check names and tickets but not bags.

sections.title: The ACL Data Model
sections.content:
The acls container holds a list of acl entries. Each ACL has a name, an optional type and a list of aces, and each ACE is indexed by its own name. An ACE contains matches and actions. ACL types are defined as identities, such as IPv4, IPv6, Ethernet and mixed types, and features select which of them a system supports. The ACE inherits the type of its ACL, which guards against misconfiguring ACE types inside an ACL.

Inside matches, choice statements select one header at each of the l2, l3 and l4 levels: Ethernet; IPv4 or IPv6; and TCP, UDP or ICMP. The ACE can also match on the egress or ingress interface. For ports, a rule gives either a lower and upper port (a range that includes both ends) or an operator together with one port.

The actions container holds a forwarding action, which is one of the identities accept, drop (without any ICMP error message) or reject (drop and send an ICMP error message to the source). It also holds an optional logging action, log-syslog or log-none.

The model also covers attachment and counting. An attachment-points container binds ACLs to an interface, with separate ingress and egress ACL sets. Statistics of matched packets and matched octets can be kept per ACE or per interface, and feature statements show which is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: A list has a name and numbered rules. Each rule says what to look for and whether to let the packet pass, throw it away quietly, or throw it away and tell the sender.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives configurations in XML and, for the first, an equivalent command-line form. The first requirement is to deny TCP traffic from 192.0.2.0/24 to 198.51.100.0/24. It is an IPv4 ACL with one ACE that matches protocol 6 and the two networks and has the forwarding action drop.

The second requirement is to accept all DNS traffic destined for 2001:db8::/32 on port 53. It is an IPv6 ACL with one ACE that matches the destination network and a UDP destination port with operator eq and port 53, with the forwarding action accept.

A third example drops TCP traffic from source ports 16384, 16385, 16386 and 16387, to show range usage. Appendix A shows how to extend the model with a company's proprietary module, with Linux nftables, and with Ethertypes.
sections.plainLanguage: One example says "block these visitors from that street", and another says "always let in anyone asking for the phone book on door 53".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data is meant to be accessed with a network management protocol such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell (SSH) for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF. The NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can limit which users reach which operations and content.

The writable data nodes can be sensitive. Unauthorized write access to /acls/acl/aces can let intruders permit traffic that should be blocked, which may result in a DoS attack or compromise the device, or deny traffic that should be allowed, which may result in a DoS attack. Unauthorized read access shows which rules are in effect and helps an attacker craft an attack.

Unauthorized write access to /acls/acl/aces/ace/actions/logging can turn on logging for many ACEs and overwhelm the server. Unauthorized read access to it can expose logging information.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger can edit the guest list, they can let in the wrong people or lock out the right ones. So only trusted people should get to change it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers three URIs in the IETF XML Registry and three YANG modules in the YANG Module Names registry. The three are ietf-access-control-list (prefix acl), ietf-packet-fields (prefix packet-fields) and ietf-ethertypes (prefix ethertypes), each with a namespace under urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC signs the three modules into an official phone book so their names are never mixed up with anyone else's.
